newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Foreign troops may defend themselves in Albania.
newsitem.headline: Foreign troops may defend themselves in Albania.

text.p: Soldiers belonging to an Italian-led eight-nation force will have the right to defend themselves if they are attacked while distributing aid in Albania, Italy's Defence Minister said on Saturday.
"If there are attacks during the distribution of aid, the only means to guarantee results is the use of arms," Beniamino Andreatta told a news conference during a brief trip to Tirana.
"Weapons will be used for self-protection," he added.

Albania sank into near-anarchy after the collapse of get-rich-quick investment schemes earlier this year, provoking a wave of popular anger. Local newspapers on Saturday put the death toll from six weeks of unrest at 279.
The United Nations has approved a 6,000-strong multinational force to protect the distribution of emergency food and aid in Albania.
The mission will include soldiers from France, Austria, Denmark, Greece, Turkey, Spain and Romania, officials said.
Albanian Defence Minister Shaqir Vukaj said Albania ran no risk of slipping into civil war.
"There is no basis for civil war in Albania because in history Albanians have not killed each other for regional, religious or political reasons," he said.
Andreatta called for elections soon in Albania, during the mandate of the mission, which could last about six months.
"It would be a dramatic situation if the force pulled out before elections were held," he said.
Andreatta said that a final decision would be taken in Rome on Monday assigning troops from each country to key locations across the country.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi was expected to visit Tirana on Sunday to underline his support for the mission and would hold a news conference at 1200 GMT, one official said.
Advance troops of the mission have already landed in Tirana to plot the arrival of the bulk of the force.

Some 100 Italian troops had arrived since Friday and most of them were protecting Tirana airport and adapting it for round-the-clock operations, one official said. A unit of some 20 men arrived in the western port of Durres on Friday.

Small numbers of Spanish, Greek, Turkish and Austrian soldiers had reached Tirana, military sources and residents said. An advance unit of about 100 French soldiers arrived in the southern Italian port of Brindisi on Friday.
Albania's King Leka I, who returned home from exile to a tumultuous welcome, gave guarded support to the force.
"As long as they come here with good will, on a mission of peace, I welcome them," he told a news conference.
"But should there be any action to change the situation, we will have to give that a second thought," he added.
